Algorithms that convey to a user issues with the sensitivity of a survey as it relates to the SDF result, or that produce quantitative uncertainty estimates in real-time do not (yet) exist, but are in active development, and would be beneficial the SDF technology, broadly. Toward quantitative error estimates, LBNL undertook a series of benchmarking measurements summarized in Refs. [33, 34] and whose analyses were completed in Ref. [35], which leveraged regularization methods first described in Ref. [36]. The measurements demonstrated that one could use an arrangement of point-like radiation sources to emulate a continuous distribution and the analyses consider the utility of using regularization approaches to add constraints to the ML- EM problem by altering the posterior probability prior as indicated in Eq. 9. The regularization functions that were considered included L , which is designed to promote sparse solutions to 1/2 Eq. 4 [37], and the Total Variation (TV) method, which attempts to add smoothness to the image space [38, 39]. In the scenarios described in Ref. [34] both regularization approaches proved beneficial to the overall image quality (as defined in Ref. [35]). These scenarios consisted of a distributed source with substantial activity, relative to a background distribution that was fairly uniform throughout the survey area. However, any prior that induces sparsity is fraught when applied to data with substantial distributed source activity in portions of the geometry where sampling is sparse. Fig. 8 illustrates this point by showing four reconstructions of the same data, but the top row is using the L regularizer while the bottom row is unregularized ML-EM. Clearly, the shape of the ML-EM solutions are not significantly altered by introduction of the background term, but an emission rate approximately 5000 γ/s/voxel activity (or ≈ 3pCi/g uranium activity) was being attributed as ‘background’. Conversely, without the fixed background term,theL MAP-EMsolutionachievesitsbestfitbyattributingsubstantialbackgroundactivity 1/2 to sparse portions of the point-cloud, near (x,y)=(10m,-10m). These L sparse background fits 1/2 are inaccurate and could distract a user and could cause an autonomous algorithm to prioritize assessment of ‘source-looking’ signatures that were actually benign background. Conversely, when the background term is fit, the regularized solution (top-right graphic in Fig. 8) best highlights the portion of the geometry that contained high-activity material, highlighting how such regularization can be beneficial, if applied properly. Further study into regularization approaches that are appropriate for given detection scenarios, better quantification of regularizer appropriateness, and further work on determining reconstruction uncertainties when using with such regularization schemes are all of value.
